card: Paper card. Question: How do the strength, ductility, and fracture toughness of an equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy compare to high-entropy alloys and conventional materials, particularly at cryogenic temperatures, and what mechanisms drive these properties?. System: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA). Processing: Arc-melted high-purity elements (>99.9%) under argon, drop-cast into copper moulds, homogenized at 1,200 °C for 24 h, cold-forged and cross-rolled to ~10 mm thickness (60% reduction), then annealed at 800 °C for 1 h in air to achieve a recrystallized microstructure with 5–50 μm grains.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at 293 K, 198 K, and 77 K with a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹; Compact-tension (C(T)) fracture toughness tests at 293 K, 198 K, and 77 K with fatigue pre-cracking and side-grooving per ASTM E1820.. Findings: At 77 K, yield strength reached 657 MPa and ultimate tensile strength reached 1,311 MPa, representing a ~50% increase from room temperature.; Tensile ductility (failure strain) increased to ~0.9 (90%) at 77 K, a ~25% increase from room temperature.; Fracture toughness (KJIc) at crack initiation increased from 208 MPa m1/2 at 293 K to 273 MPa m1/2 at 77 K.; Crack-growth toughness at 77 K reached critical stress-intensity values of ~430 MPa m1/2 (J ~900 kJ m⁻²).; The alloy exhibited a high strain-hardening exponent (n) of 0.4 at cryogenic temperatures.; The CrCoNi alloy showed ~15% higher tensile strength, ~30% higher ductility, and ~50% higher work of fracture than the five-component CrMnFeCoNi alloy at room temperature.; At 77 K, the CrCoNi alloy displayed ~25% higher KJIc, ~27% higher ductility, and ~31% higher work of fracture compared to the CrMnFeCoNi alloy.. Mechanism: The exceptional damage tolerance results from continuous steady strain hardening that suppresses plastic instability, driven by pronounced dislocation activity and deformation-induced nano-twinning. Nano-twinning acts as a dominant deformation mode that provides a steady source of strain hardening, delaying necking and accommodating strain, with its intensity increasing as temperature decreases from room temperature to 77 K.. Limitations: The yield strength at 77 K was slightly lower than the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, attributed to the non-uniform grain size of the current material; the volume fraction of void-initiating inclusions was not accurately quantified relative to the five-component alloy.. Future work: Further studies are needed to accurately determine the relative volume fractions of void-initiating inclusions in the MEA and HEA and to identify their chemistry and crystal structure by TEM after extraction from the voids.. Quote: "strength, ductility and toughness of the CrCoNi alloy improve to strength levels above 1.3 GPa, failure strains up to 90% and KJIc values of 275 MPa m1/2."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the atomistic to micro-scale mechanisms underlying the exceptional damage tolerance (high strength, ductility, and fracture toughness) of the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy?. System: CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (single-phase fcc solid solution). Processing: Arc-melting high-purity elemental starting materials, drop casting into copper moulds, cold forging and cross rolling at room temperature, recrystallization at 800 °C (grain size ∼6 μm), followed by ion milling (5 kV) or twin jet polishing (10 °C, 13 mA/12 V) to create electron-transparent foils with cracks. Test conditions: In situ straining in an aberration-corrected TEM (FEI Tecnai G2 F20, 200 kV) at room temperature using pulsed tensile loading (axial displacement rate ∼1.0 μm s⁻¹). Findings: Early deformation is dominated by the easy motion of Shockley partial dislocations (1/6<112> type) and the continuous nucleation/annihilation of stacking faults (SFs).; Interactions between partials on different {111} planes form stable 'stacking-fault parallelepipeds' (volume defects) that act as formidable obstacles for dislocation motion.; Perfect (undissociated, 1/2<110> type) dislocations move with extreme difficulty in localized bands of planar slip, creating strong barriers that arrest fast-moving partial dislocations.; The motion of perfect dislocations requires overcoming continuous activation barriers, indicative of high friction stress in the alloy.; Nanoscale voids form in the 'semi-cohesive zone' at the intersection of two {111} slip planes, creating fiber-like bridges spanning the crack faces.; These nanobridges (size <200 nm, some ∼100 nm) deform primarily via nano-twinning ({111} twin structure), which accommodates strain and shields the crack tip.; The synergy of these mechanisms yields tensile strength ∼1 GPa, ductility ∼60–70%, and fracture toughness K_JIc > 200 MPa√m.. Mechanism: The authors propose a synergistic sequence where intrinsic toughening arises from easy partial dislocation motion (ductility) followed by strain hardening via stacking-fault parallelepipeds and planar slip bands (strength). Extrinsic toughening occurs via nanoscale twinned bridges that form behind the crack tip, carrying load and shielding the crack tip from the applied driving force.. Limitations: The study notes that 'ultrahigh-resolution observations have to be made at the nanoscale to permit any characterization of mechanisms so close to the crack tip,' and that 'thin foil samples must be used which, under load, cannot display the full constraint of a bulk sample.'. Future work: The authors state that 'further optimization of these mechanisms may present new directions for the future design of advanced metallic materials with unprecedented damage tolerance.'. Quote: "We identify a synergy of multiple deformation mechanisms, rarely achieved in metallic alloys, which generates high strength, work hardening and ductility"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength–ductility synergy in eutectic high-entropy alloys be improved by inheriting the composite lamellar nature through tailored thermo-mechanical processing?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (at%) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Arc-melting followed by suction-casting into a copper mold, multi-pass cold-rolling to 84–86% reduction in thickness, and non-isothermal annealing at 660, 700, 740, or 900 °C for 1 h with a heating rate of 10 °C min−1 followed by water quenching.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests with an initial strain rate of 2.5 × 10−4 s−1 using dog-bone specimens (15 mm gauge length, 3.2 mm width, 600 μm thickness) and loading–unloading–reloading (LUR) tests.. Findings: The DPHL700 and DPHL740 samples achieved a yield strength of approximately 1.5 GPa with an elongation of ~16%, representing a simultaneous enhancement in both strength and ductility compared to as-cast and ultrafine-grained counterparts.; The microstructure exhibited a two-hierarchical heterogeneity consisting of submicron-grade FCC/B2 grains within FCC lamellae and micron-grade alternate FCC/B2 lamellae.; The average diameters of FCC and B2 grains were roughly comparable at ~0.71 μm, with inter-lamella spacings ranging from 1.5 to 5 μm.; Phase decomposition resulted in two types of NiAl-rich precipitates in FCC lamellae: small intragranular P1 grains (50–180 nm) and large intergranular P2 grains (~350 nm).; Back-stress measurements at the yield point reached ~950 MPa, which was approximately 3 times higher than the effective stress, primarily responsible for the high yield strength.; The strain-hardening rate (Θ) showed a transient behavior with an up-turn in region II and sustained high Θ over a wide strain region III for DPHL700.; Microcrack-arresting mechanisms were observed where multiple microcracks were inhibited from coalescing, with ductile components acting as efficient crack arresters.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the enhanced properties to a two-hierarchical constraint effect that generates long-range back-stress by storing geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) due to strain gradients at lamella interfaces and around intergranular precipitates, combined with a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism where the aligned lamellar architecture delays crack propagation and coalescence.. Limitations: The authors note that while the DPHL structure is effective, increasing the annealing temperature to 900 °C induced a partially degraded lamellar structure that led to inferior tensile properties, indicating the sensitivity of the process to thermal treatment.. Future work: The authors propose that further efforts should be devoted to exploring non-equiatomic alloys and spinodal decomposition to create low-misfit coherent nanostructures for even higher yield strengths, and anticipate modifying the EHEA to satisfy requirements for high-temperature and/or corrosion environments.. W2150567030.title: Heterogeneous lamella structure unites ultrafine-grain strength with coarse-grain ductility

card: Paper card. Question: How to achieve a simultaneous balance of high fracture strength and high ductility in high-entropy alloys while overcoming inferior castability and compositional segregation?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of commercially pure elements (Al, Co, Ni: 99.9 wt.%; Cr, Fe: 99.5 ~ 99.6 wt.%) in a BN crucible; heating to 600°C for 1 hour; pouring at 1500°C into a MgO crucible (220 mm length, 62 mm upper ID, 50 mm bottom ID) under argon atmosphere (0.06 MPa); bulk ingot weight ~2.5 kg.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; elevated temperature tests at 600°C and 700°C at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; cold rolling with 8% thickness reduction followed by tensile testing at 2 × 10−3 s−1.. Findings: The as-cast alloy exhibited a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with an inter-lamellar spacing of about 2 μm.; Room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%.; The proof stress was 75 MPa, while the fracture stress reached close to 1.2 GPa (true stress condition).; At 600°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 806 MPa and elongation of 33.7%.; At 700°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 538 MPa and elongation of 22.9%.; Cold rolling with 8% reduction increased the true fracture stress to 1265 MPa while maintaining 9.9% elongation.; The density of the EHEA was measured to be 7.38 g/cm3.; The ratio of fracture strength to proof stress (σUTS/σ0.2) was close to 16.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the unprecedented strain hardening and balanced properties to the fine regular lamellar structure that easily stores dislocations and the alternating soft fcc phases and hard B2-structured NiAl-rich phases. When dislocations pass through soft fcc phases, the hard B2 phases, including nanoscale precipitates, pin the movement of dislocations resulting in significant work hardening.. Limitations: The text notes that the mechanism for the low elastic limit (proof stress) is still unclear at this stage.. Future work: Further exploration of new EHEAs will be based on physical metallurgy principles using atomic radius, mixing enthalpy, and valence electron concentration; thermodynamics calculations based on the CALPHAD method can provide guidance once reliable databases are established; the potential for producing ultrahigh strength components after large plastic deformation awaits further investigations.. Quote: "To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases."

W2622849719.title: Phase‐Transformation Ductilization of Brittle High‐Entropy Alloys via Metastability Engineering

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloys be designed to achieve ultra-high strength while retaining good ductility, overcoming the limitation of near-equiatomic compositions that restrict the formation of high-volume fractions of ductile strengthening precipitates?. System: Al0.5Cr0.9FeNi2.5V0.2 (non-equiatomic, ~50 at% Ni, ~18 at% Cr, ~4 at% V). Processing: Arc-melting pure metals, casting into copper mold, solution-treating at 1200 °C for 24 h followed by water quenching, cold-rolling with 72% reduction ratio, and ageing at 600 °C or 700 °C for 1 h followed by air cooling.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 on dog-bone-shaped samples (gauge length 10 mm, width 3 mm, thickness 1 mm).. Findings: Achieved an ultrahigh yield strength of 1810 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 1905 MPa in the sample aged at 600 °C.; The strength increment relative to the solution-treated sample was >1500 MPa (>560%).; Retained good ductility with elongation of ~9–10% after achieving the maximum strength.; Formed high-content ordered L12 nanoprecipitates with a volume fraction of ~50.1% in the 600 A sample.; The L12 phases are coherent with the FCC matrix, with a lattice parameter difference of only 0.0001 nm (0.3582 nm vs 0.3583 nm).; The spinodal nanostructure contributed 1158 MPa to the yield strength, while grain boundaries contributed 212 MPa.; The total estimated yield strength increase (1524 MPa) agrees closely with the experimental result (1536 MPa).; The mean diameter of the ordered L12 precipitates was determined to be ~35 nm.. Mechanism: The alloying strategy utilizes spinodal decomposition to create a low-misfit coherent nanostructure where the L12 nanophases resist dislocation motion by providing strong diffuse attractive obstacles to trap moving dislocations and by creating antiphase boundaries (APBs) on the slip planes when sheared by dislocations. The diffuse coherent interfaces minimize elastic strain accumulation, preventing crack initiation and maintaining ductility.. Limitations: The authors note that the calculated strengthening contributions based on assuming spherical precipitates may underestimate the area of APBs and the strengthening effect because the actual L12 phases are irregular and interconnected. Additionally, the volume fraction calculations may not be absolutely precise.. Future work: The authors anticipate that this alloying strategy can offer more possibilities for the compositional design of HEAs and will open new avenues for development of ultrastrong and ductile HEAs superior to existing commercial alloys, potentially competing with traditional structural materials in rigorous service conditions.. Quote: "Here we present a strategy to design ultrastrong HEAs with high-content nanoprecipitates by phase separation, which can generate a near-equiatomic matrix in situ while forming strengthening phases"

W2893800769.title: High-content ductile coherent nanoprecipitates achieve ultrastrong high-entropy alloys

card: Paper card. Question: How can a single-phase face-centered cubic medium-entropy alloy achieve both gigapascal yield strength and high uniform ductility without relying on second-phase heterogeneities?. System: Equimolar CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (33.48Cr-32.46Co-34.06Ni atomic percent). Processing: Electromagnetic levitation melting, homogenization at 1,473 K for 12 h, hot forging (1,323–1,173 K), cold rolling to 0.5 mm sheets, followed by partial recrystallization annealing at 873 K for 1 h and water quenching. Test conditions: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests at strain rate 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, room temperature (298 K) and liquid nitrogen temperature (77 K); loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tests to measure back stresses. Findings: Yield strength (σ0.2) of ~1,150 MPa achieved with a three-level heterogeneous grain structure (HGS) spanning nanometer to micrometer scales.; Uniform tensile strain (Eu) reached 22% at room temperature, significantly higher than the ~2% Eu observed in homogeneous ultrafine-grained counterparts with similar strength.; The number density of nanograins (ρNG) increased from 4.7 grains/µm² before testing to 21 grains/µm² after deformation at 298 K and 31 grains/µm² at 77 K.; Back stress hardening accounted for over 80% of the total stress elevation observed during strain hardening from yield to ultimate tensile stress.; The strain hardening rate (Θ) exhibited a distinct upturn between 4% and 8% strain, contrasting with the monotonic drop seen in homogeneous structures.; The width of hysteresis loops in LUR tests was the largest ever recorded for any known alloy, indicating exceptionally high internal back stresses.; Corner twins evolved into nanograins during tensile straining, dynamically reinforcing the heterogeneity of the grain structure.. Mechanism: The heterogeneous grain structure induces load partitioning and strain gradient hardening, causing dislocation pile-ups at grain boundaries and generating geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs). This creates large long-range internal back stresses that sustain strain hardening. Additionally, the low stacking fault energy facilitates the dynamic generation of twinned nanograins at grain boundaries during deformation, which further refines the structure and perpetuates back stress hardening.. Limitations: The beneficial effects of the HGS diminish if the material undergoes extended annealing toward uniform grains or if the alloy has high stacking fault energy where full dislocations dominate and recover/annihilate easily.. Future work: The authors propose that this strategy is generally applicable to other single-phase low-SFE alloys and metals to achieve simultaneous high yield strength and high tensile ductility.. Quote: "This heterogeneity results from this alloy's low stacking fault energy, which facilitates corner twins in recrystallization and stores deformation twins and stacking faults during tensile straining."

W2302110147.title: Strain hardening in Fe–16Mn–10Al–0.86C–5Ni high specific strength steel

card: Paper card. Question: How can cryo-rolling and annealing be utilized to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in multiphase high entropy alloys, specifically regarding the development of a hierarchical microstructure?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Multi-pass cryo-rolling up to ~90% reduction in thickness with immersion in liquid N2 for 45 minutes before and after each pass, followed by annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour and water quenching.. Test conditions: Tensile tests at ambient temperature with an initial strain rate of 8.3 × 10−4 s−1; Nano-indentation with load increased linearly from 1 μN to 500 μN over 0.25 seconds.. Findings: The cryo-rolled and annealed material achieved a Yield Strength (YS) of 1437 ± 26 MPa and Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS) of 1562 ± 33 MPa.; The elongation to failure (ef) was approximately 14 ± 1%, which remained almost unchanged compared to the as-cast material (17 ± 1%).; The hierarchical microstructure consists of fine lamellar regions with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and coarse non-lamellar regions with coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm).; The hardness of the B2 phase (~12 GPa) is nearly three times higher than that of the L12 phase (~4 GPa) in the as-cast material.; The cryo-rolled and annealed material covers the entire hardness spectrum with softer regions (≤8 GPa), intermediate regions (~8–12 GPa), and much harder regions (≥12 GPa).; The cold-rolled and annealed material showed a homogenous microduplex morphology with grain sizes of ~0.5 µm, unlike the heterogeneous cryo-rolled structure.; The cryo-rolled and annealed EHEA possesses the highest YS and UTS while maintaining appreciable ductility compared to other HEAs like Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi and Fe40Mn27Ni26Co5Cr2.. Mechanism: The simultaneous enhancement in strength and ductility originates from a characteristic hierarchical microstructure that creates profuse domain boundaries separating domains of different hardness, leading to significant back stress strengthening and delayed necking due to strain gradients and geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs).. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work.. Quote: "The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%)"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength–ductility trade-off inherent to traditional alloys be overcome in multi-principal-element alloys by exploiting multiple levels of heterogeneities?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) and medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) including FCC-based systems (e.g., CoCrFeNi, CrCoNi, VCoNi), BCC-based refractory systems (e.g., TiZrHfNbTa), dual-phase eutectic lamella HEAs, and alloys with multicomponent intermetallic nanoparticles (MCINPs). Processing: Partial recrystallization to create heterogeneous grain structures (HGS), spinodal decomposition to form precipitates, addition of oxygen solutes (~2 at%) to form nanoscale complexes, and intentional alloying to tune stacking fault energy (SFE) for deformation-induced transformations. Test conditions: Room temperature (RT) uniaxial tensile testing; cryogenic temperatures (77 K and 4 K) for specific FCC MEAs; compression testing for some refractory BCC HEAs. Findings: An FCC-MCINP alloy achieved a yield strength above 1 GPa with a uniform elongation (εu) of ~50%, showing no strength–ductility trade-off compared to unstrengthened elemental metals.; A single-phase CrCoNi MEA with a heterogeneous grain structure (HGS) spanning nano-to-micro scales reached a gigapascal yield strength while maintaining εu in excess of 20%.; The VCoNi MEA achieved near-GPa yield strength with εu ~30% and total elongation ~38%, attributed to maximized lattice friction from atomic size mismatch.; In BCC-TiZrHfNb HEA, adding ~2 at% oxygen formed nanoscale (O, Ti, Zr)-complexes that increased tensile elongation from ~14% to ~28% while maintaining high strength.; Stress-assisted martensitic transformation in BCC-Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5 HEA created a 65% volume fraction of internally twinned martensite, doubling the strain-hardening rate.; Wide hysteresis loops in load–unload–reload stress–strain curves demonstrated that nonhomogeneous plastic deformation in HGS alloys imparts high back stresses contributing to strain hardening.; At cryogenic temperatures (77 K and 4 K), the CrCoNi MEA exhibited strain-hardening rates and εu comparable to the best 316 austenitic stainless steels due to reduced dynamic recovery.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high concentration of multiple principal elements creates a rugged energy landscape with statistical fluctuations in composition and local chemical order (LCO), causing dislocations to adopt a wavy line and face intermittent 'nanoscale segment detrapping' barriers. This intrinsic lattice friction is compounded by a hierarchy of heterogeneities (defects, precipitates, grain boundaries, phase boundaries) that promote nonhomogeneous plastic deformation, geometrically necessary dislocation storage, and dynamic mechanisms like twinning (TWIP) and transformation (TRIP), which sustain high strain-hardening rates to delay necking.. Limitations: Refractory BCC HEAs often lack room-temperature tensile ductility due to a drastic rise in the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature; TRIP-assisted DP alloys with low initial yield strength require hardening (e.g., cold work) which causes the strain-hardening rate to become inadequate, restoring the strength–ductility trade-off at high σy levels.. Future work: Continued endeavors to tailor heterogeneities to ward off plastic instabilities and realize even better strength–ductility balance, expanding the repertoire of alloys in compositions and properties through refined and enhanced HEAs.. Quote: "The strength of HEAs is considerably higher than traditional solid solutions, as the many constituents lead to a rugged energy landscape that increases the resistance to dislocation motion."

W2805419750.title: Tunable stacking fault energies by tailoring local chemical order in CrCoNi medium-entropy alloys

card: Paper card. Question: What distinguishes multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) from traditional solid solutions, and how does local chemical order (LCO) influence dislocation behavior and mechanical strength?. System: FCC NiCoCr medium-entropy alloy (equiatomic composition). Processing: Hybrid molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations with annealing temperatures (Ta) ranging from 650 K to 1650 K; empirical embedded-atom method (EAM) potential developed without spin polarization; simulation box ~52 nm × 6 nm × 52 nm with 1,584,000 atomic sites; 270,000–500,000 MC cycles for convergence.. Test conditions: Energy pathway calculations at 0 K; dislocation motion simulations at 300 K under constant shear stress of 300 MPa; strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 for CRSS estimation; activation barrier calculations via minimum energy path (MEP).. Findings: Configurational entropy (Sc) rarely reaches the ideal value (Sc,ideal); at 1650 K, Sc is ~95% of Sc,ideal, but drops significantly as LCO develops at lower Ta.; Complex stacking fault energy (CSFE) varies from -24.0 mJ/m² (random solid solution) to ~57 mJ/m² (strong LCO at 650 K).; Local antiphase boundary energies (APBEs) increase from ~50 mJ/m² to ~112 mJ/m² as Ta decreases from 1650 K to 650 K.; Twin boundary energy (γB) in LCO samples increases linearly with the number of transformed layers (λ), unlike elemental FCC metals where it converges.; Dislocations move via intermittent nanoscale segment detrapping (NSD) rather than smooth propagation, with effective barriers of ~0.15 eV even at 400 MPa shear stress.; Shear stress required to drive dislocation motion increases by a factor of three when the alloy is annealed at 650 K compared to the random state.; Critical resolved shear strength (CRSS) for the random NiCoCr state is ~70 MPa at 300 K and 10^-3 s^-1, consistent with experimental values of ~69 ± 3 MPa.. Mechanism: LCO creates a rugged energy landscape with spatially heterogeneous complex stacking fault energies (CSFE) and antiphase boundary energies (APBE). This heterogeneity acts as nanoscale obstacles that trap dislocation segments, forcing them to move via a nanoscale segment detrapping (NSD) mechanism. The energy required to break LCOs during slip and twinning increases activation barriers and lattice friction, leading to strengthening.. Limitations: The study uses a non-magnetic EAM potential which does not explicitly consider spin polarization; magnetic effects could alter energy differences by ~15 meV/atom. The simulations assume a single-phase solution without second-phase precipitation. Kinetic limitations in experiments may prevent the formation of predicted LCO states at low temperatures within typical homogenization times.. Future work: The authors propose using rapid cooling to obtain a random solid solution for ductility, followed by aging at elevated temperatures to induce LCO for strength. They suggest that the variability in LCO offers a new knob for property tuning in single-phase alloys.. Quote: "The LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities."

Paper card. Question: How does local chemical order (LCO) affect local dislocation segment activation barriers in multi-principal element alloys?. System: Multi-principal element alloys (specifically samples with equilibrium LCOs at Ta = 650, 950, and 1350 K). Processing: Hybrid MD and MC simulations on 20 nm × 20 nm × 10 nm samples (30 samples per condition) at Ta = 650, 950, and 1350 K; quenched to 0 K; cylinder configurations (20 nm diameter, 10 nm length) cut with a partial dislocation of screw character introduced; quasi-static athermal shearing employed; MEPs calculated using the simplified and improved string method with FIRE algorithm (reparameterization every 10 increments, convergence <10–3 Å or 3000 iterations). Test conditions: Temperatures of 650 K, 950 K, and 1350 K for equilibrium LCO; 0 K for energy minimization; athermal stress limit via quasi-static shearing. Findings: 30 different samples were obtained for each processing condition to ensure meaningful statistics; Sample dimensions were 20 nm × 20 nm × 10 nm along x[11¯0], y[1¯1¯1¯], and z[112¯]; Cylinder configurations had a diameter of 20 nm and axial direction along [112¯]; Dislocation line length was 10 nm as detrapping processes are on the nanoscale; Outer layers of atoms with thickness >2x potential cutoff radius were fixed during energy minimization; Inner cylindrical region with 10 nm diameter was used to calculate average local shear stress; Convergence criterion for MEP calculation was displacement <10–3 Å or 3000 iterations. Mechanism: The authors employed hybrid MD and MC simulations to obtain equilibrium LCOs and then used the string method to calculate minimum energy pathways (MEPs) for dislocation segments, aiming to examine LCO effects on local dislocation segment activation barriers.. Quote: "In order to examine the LCO effects on local dislocation segment activation barriers, hybrid MD and MC simulations were performed"

W2936950287.title: Strengthening in multi-principal element alloys with local-chemical-order roughened dislocation pathways

card: Paper card. Question: How does the capacity for twinning-controlled deformation in the equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy generate a simultaneous increase in strength and ductility, and what is the origin of its exceptional fracture toughness?. System: Nominally equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with a single-phase face-centered cubic (fcc) structure. Processing: Samples extracted from a previously produced alloy; micro-pillars (~300 nm diameter) machined using focused-ion beam (FIB) techniques; in situ TEM compression tests performed at 300 kV; in situ TEM tensile tests conducted at room temperature using a Gatan model 654 single-tilt straining holder at 200 kV; DFT calculations performed using VASP with the nudged-elastic band method. Test conditions: Room temperature (300 K); uniaxial tension and compression; micro-pillar compression at 300 kV; in situ straining at 10 frames per second; DFT calculations at 0 K and 500 K. Findings: The alloy exhibits high strength (~1 GPa), ductility (~60% uniform elongation), and exceptional fracture toughness (KIc > 200 MPa√m).; Ab initio calculations reveal a negative intrinsic stacking-fault energy (γisf = −23 mJ m−2) at 0 K and a high twinnability value (τta = 1.07 ± 0.02).; Deformation activates three twinning systems within individual coarse grains (5–50 μm), forming a stable 3D hierarchical twin network with twin thicknesses ranging from ~100 nm to several micrometres.; Micro-pillars containing a pre-existing {111} twin boundary showed a maximum strength exceeding 2.5 GPa, approximately 1 GPa higher than pillars without a twin.; Dislocations pile up at coherent twin boundaries (CTBs), acting as strong barriers to motion, while intersecting twin boundaries serve as fast channels for dislocation glide.; Dislocations cross-slip between intersecting twin boundaries via an 'overpass' mechanism, enabling homogeneous plastic deformation in three dimensions.; The 3D twin architecture remains stable during deformation with no evidence of twin growth or de-twinning, even as dislocations move rapidly along the boundaries.. Mechanism: The 3D hierarchical twin network provides a dual function: conventional strengthening occurs via the blockage of dislocations impinging on twin boundaries, while the interconnected network offers pathways for dislocation glide along and cross-slip between intersecting twin-matrix interfaces, allowing simultaneous high strength and ductility.. Limitations: The study notes that nano-pillar tests investigate limited volumes; detailed processes of sessile dislocation involvement in cross-slip were not fully captured due to limited time-resolution of in situ TEM; the specific role of magnetization was analyzed but calculations were mainly performed on non-magnetic structures.. Future work: The authors propose that documenting this enhanced twinning-induced toughness may present new directions for the future design of metallic alloys with unprecedented combinations of mechanical properties.. Quote: "This serves a dual function: conventional twin-boundary (TB) strengthening from blockage of dislocations impinging on TBs, coupled with the 3D twin network which offers pathways for dislocation glide along, and cross-slip between, intersecting TB-matrix interfaces."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the origin of the superior strength and plasticity in the CrCoNi alloy compared to the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, and how do magnetic properties influence the phase stability between fcc and hcp structures?. System: CrCoNi (ternary), CrMnFeCoNi (quinary), FeCoNi, MnCoNi, MnFeNi (equiatomic ternary derivatives). Processing: Alloys prepared as single-phase fcc solid solutions; samples deformed to approximately 55% true strain; DFT calculations using VASP with GGA-PBE, quasi-harmonic approximation for vibrational entropy, and special quasi-random structures (SQS); atomistic simulations using classical potentials on fcc Co as a surrogate.. Test conditions: Cryogenic to room temperature regimes relevant to experiments; shear deformations inducing stacking faults and twin interfaces; magnetic and non-magnetic DFT calculations; atomic resolution STEM in HAADF mode along 110 and 101 zone axes.. Findings: CrCoNi exhibits a distinctly lower-energy hcp phase compared to fcc at low temperatures, driven by vibrational entropy, whereas CrMnFeCoNi shows negligible energy difference due to magnetic frustration.; In CrCoNi, the hcp phase is favored over fcc even when magnetic effects are turned off, while in Mn-containing alloys (MnCoNi, MnFeNi), magnetism reduces the energy difference between phases to nearly zero.; Mn atoms exhibit magnetic frustration with moments fluctuating between approximately 3 and -3 μB regardless of environment, unlike Cr moments which show a narrower distribution and stronger dependence on local chemistry.; The average stacking fault energy in CrCoNi is negative, indicating a driving force for fcc-to-hcp transformation, whereas in CrMnFeCoNi, energy overlaps between stable and unstable structures prevent a clear driving force.; Hcp laths in CrCoNi form localized to stacking faults and twin interfaces via the glide of 1/6<112> Shockley partial dislocations, rather than as a bulk transformation.; Dislocation interactions with twin boundaries in CrCoNi lead to the nucleation of 3-layer hcp structures, which act as barriers to slip while redirecting shear to prevent stress concentration.; The hcp phase in CrCoNi can heal back to fcc upon removal of stress or interaction with intersecting slip systems, allowing for recovery without loss of plasticity.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the superior mechanical properties of CrCoNi arise from a magnetically-driven fcc-to-hcp phase transformation triggered by dislocation slip. In CrCoNi, the hcp phase is intrinsically lower in energy (ground state) at low temperatures, and the absence of magnetic frustration allows this transformation to proceed readily at stacking faults and twin boundaries. This creates nanostructured hcp laths that strengthen the material by blocking dislocations while simultaneously redirecting shear to avoid crack initiation. In contrast, the addition of Mn in CrMnFeCoNi introduces magnetic frustration, which eliminates the energy difference between fcc and hcp phases, suppressing the transformation and resulting in inferior mechanical performance.. Limitations: Free energy calculations for the quinary CrMnFeCoNi alloy pose significant practical challenges and yielded non-conclusive estimates; the study uses fcc Co as a surrogate system for atomistic simulations of dislocation interactions in CrCoNi due to the lack of reliable interatomic potentials for the Ni-Co-Cr system.. Future work: The authors suggest that new alloying combinations can be predicted based on favorable magnetic properties to design single-phase alloys with metastable structures, emphasizing that high-entropy alloys with more constituent elements are not necessarily superior to their derivatives.. Quote: "This highlights the unique combination of chemistry and magnetic properties in CrCoNi, leading to a fcc-hcp phase transformation that occurs only in this alloy."

card: Paper card. Question: Can high pressure induce a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phase in the prototypical face-centered cubic (fcc) high-entropy alloy CrMnFeCoNi, and what are the mechanisms and retention characteristics of this transformation?. System: CrMnFeCoNi (near-equiatomic solid solution of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni). Processing: Arc-melting of equimolar constituent metals under Ar, drop casting, annealing at 1,200 °C for 24 h, powdering, and loading into a diamond anvil cell with silicone oil pressure medium and Au pressure standard; pressure increased stepwise to 54.1 GPa and decreased at ~1 GPa min⁻¹. Test conditions: Ambient temperature, pressures up to 54.1 GPa, angle-dispersive X-ray diffraction (λ=0.4959 Å). Findings: The fcc-to-hcp transformation begins at approximately 14 GPa.; The transformation is sluggish, occurring over a pressure range of >40 GPa.; The volume collapse accompanying the transformation is 0.6(4)%.; The bulk modulus of the initial fcc phase is 150(3) GPa.; The bulk modulus of the high-pressure hcp phase is 141(8) GPa.; Upon decompression from 54.1 GPa, 56(2)% of the material remains in the hcp phase at ambient pressure.; Upon decompression from 26.8 GPa, 34(1)% of the material remains in the hcp phase at ambient pressure.; Roughly 60% of the hcp volume is retained after depressurization regardless of the maximum pressure achieved.. Mechanism: The transformation is driven by the pressure-induced suppression of local magnetic moments (primarily Fe), which destabilizes the fcc structure; the sluggish kinetics are attributed to the proportionality between pressure and the energy barrier for stacking fault formation.. Limitations: The text notes that the hcp phase is retained due to kinetic hindrance (trapping of atoms and lattice strain) rather than thermodynamic stability, and that rapid pressure quenching might be needed to enhance retention.. Future work: The authors suggest that removing Fe from the alloy might enhance hcp stability and reduce the critical pressure for formation, and that high-pressure processing could be used to tailor mixtures of hard hcp and ductile fcc phases.. Quote: "This martensitic transformation begins at 14 GPa and is attributed to suppression of the local magnetic moments, destabilizing the initial fcc structure."

card: Paper card. Question: How local chemistry affects enhanced deformation mechanisms and the origin of strain hardening in dual-phase high-entropy alloys.. System: Cantor-like Cr20Mn6Fe34Co34Ni6 high-entropy alloy (at.%) comprising face-centered cubic (fcc) austenite and hexagonal closed packed (hcp) ε-martensite phases.. Processing: Vacuum induction casting of 4-kg ingots, hot rolling at 900 °C (50% reduction), homogenization at 1200 °C for 3 h with water quenching, cold rolling to 40–50% thickness reduction, and recrystallization annealing at 800 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature (strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1); in situ TEM straining at ambient temperature (200 kV, loading rate ~1 μm/s); nanoscale pillar compression (300 nm diameter, 2 nm/s displacement rate).. Findings: The alloy exhibits a tensile strength approaching 1 GPa and ductility of almost 60% at ambient temperatures.; Partial dislocation activities result in stable three-dimensional stacking-fault networks comprising multiple stacking faults and sessile Lomer–Cottrell locks.; The fraction of the stronger hcp phase progressively increases during plastic deformation by forming at the stacking-fault network boundaries in the fcc phase.; Dual-phase pillars displayed the highest ultimate strength at ~3.45 GPa, compared to ~2.25 GPa for pure hcp and ~1.25 GPa for pure fcc pillars.; Local chemical composition variations show Ni atomic fraction fluctuating from −58% to 115% about its average, with Mn near stacking faults being nearly 30% higher than in the matrix.; The continuous fcc → hcp phase transformation sustains a hardening effect where flow stress increases two-fold from 1.75 to ~3.5 GPa.; Lomer–Cottrell locks act to immobilize dislocation motion and provide nucleation sites for the hcp phase transformation.. Mechanism: The authors argue that variations in local chemical composition promote a high density of Lomer-Cottrell locks, which facilitate the construction of stable 3D stacking-fault networks. These networks impede dislocation motion (work hardening) and serve as preferred sites for the nucleation and growth of the hcp phase via a transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect, where the continuous increase in the hcp volume fraction drives the ultrahigh strain hardening.. Limitations: The fracture toughness of these TRIP HEAs may not be similarly enhanced compared to the Cantor alloy, particularly at decreasing temperatures, because the product hcp ε-martensite phase tends to be quite brittle.. Future work: The authors propose that the intentional generation of Lomer–Cottrell locks raises a fundamental question of how to increase the probability of interactions between dissociated dislocations with the sole objective of enhancing the formation of such locks.. Quote: "variations in local chemical composition promote a high density of Lomer-Cottrell locks, which facilitate the construction of the stacking-fault networks to provide nucleation sites for the hcp phase transformation."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the deformation mechanisms and strain-hardening behaviors of 〈001〉-oriented fcc dual-phase FeCoCrNiAl0.5 at room and cryogenic temperatures?. System: FeCoCrNiAl0.5 (dual-phase fcc dendrites with bcc/B2 interdendritic network and precipitates). Processing: Bridgman technique ingot preparation in Ar atmosphere, homogenization at 1373K for 24 h, annealing at 1123K for 1 h, water quench, electro-discharge machining (EDM) to 4 mm × 4 mm × 8 mm, grinding to 4000 grit, vibration-polishing for EBSD. Test conditions: Uniaxial compression at 77K (liquid nitrogen) and 293K (room temperature) up to ~35% total axial strain; ex-situ digital image correlation (DIC) with 0.08 μm/pixel resolution; EBSD and TEM analysis. Findings: Hardening rate saturates at ~6 GPa above 23% total axial strain at both 77K and 293K.; Stress levels exceed 1800 MPa at ~35% total axial strain without failure at either temperature.; The fcc component carries the larger part of the plastic strain (mean strain ~3% in fcc vs ~1% in bcc/B2 at ~2% total strain).; Deformation twinning is observed in the fcc phase at both 77K and 293K, but only above 23% axial strain.; Slip activity is found exclusively in the bcc/B2 phase, with no deformation twinning observed there.; Increasing temperature from 77K to 293K raises stress levels by 250–350 MPa but leaves the hardening rate variation unaffected.; The hardening rate increase of >2 GPa beyond 23% strain is present even at room temperature.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the substantial hardening to the combined action of fcc–bcc/B2 interphase boundaries acting as obstacles, extensive deformation twinning in the fcc phase which strongly hardens secondary systems, and fine dense bcc/B2 precipitates inside the fcc dendrites. They specifically note that twin-related interactions are far more important for strengthening than pure slip interactions, and that dislocation reactions at fcc-bcc/B2 interfaces and fcc twin boundaries create residual barriers.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that the intricate microstructure and chemical gradients add intricacy to the stress-strain response and that further work is needed to unravel the influence of the minor phase volume fraction and distribution.. Future work: The authors propose that future work should focus on in-situ DIC, nanomechanical testing, and varying heterointerface amounts to differentiate contributions. They also suggest work on the effects of composition on intrinsic energy barriers and composition optimization to develop novel HEAs with higher work-hardening.. Quote: "As a result, the hardening rate associated saturates at the unusual high value of ~6 GPa."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the micromechanical properties, specifically elastic stability, anisotropy, ideal shear strength, and dislocation core width, compare between fcc and hcp phases of polymorphic high-entropy alloys?. System: Five 3d transition metal HEAs: Cr25Fe25Co25Ni25, Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20, Cr20Mn20Fe30Co20Ni10, Cr20Mn20Fe34Co20Ni6, and Cr10Mn30Fe50Co10. Processing: First-principles simulations using density-functional theory (DFT) with the exact muffin-tin orbitals method (EMTO) and coherent-potential approximation (CPA); calculations performed in paramagnetic state with Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof functional. Test conditions: Zero temperature and pressure; shear loading on (111) planes for fcc and (0001) basal planes for hcp; two modes considered: no relaxation and relaxation allowed after each shear step. Findings: All five HEAs are elastically stable in both fcc and hcp phases at zero temperature and pressure.; In the hcp phase, polycrystalline moduli decrease with increasing valence electron concentration (VEC), with variations of ~38% for shear modulus G, ~36% for Young's modulus E, and ~26% for bulk modulus B.; In the fcc phase, Young's modulus E and shear modulus G reduce until VEC reaches ≈ 8, then slightly increase.; For VEC ≤ 8, hcp phases exhibit larger Young's modulus E, bulk modulus B, and shear modulus G than their fcc counterparts.; The ideal shear strength (ISS) of hcp Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 is 11.7 GPa, which is more than two times larger than its fcc phase value of 4.4 GPa.; Relaxation during shearing reduces the ISS by 22% for Cr20Mn20Fe30Co20Ni10 and 20% for Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 in the hcp phase.; The half-width of the dislocation core (ζ) for fcc Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 is 3.89 Å, which is more than two times larger than the ζ values of 1.57 Å and 1.53 Å for the hcp phases of Cr20Mn20Fe30Co20Ni10 and Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20, respectively.; The fcc structure is elastically more anisotropic than the hcp structure across the studied alloys.. Mechanism: The higher ISS in hcp is attributed to its ABAB stacking sequence acting as an intermediate case between the 'soft' and 'hard' shear directions of fcc, leading to a more rapid energy increase. The larger dislocation core width in fcc reduces the Peierls barrier, explaining its increased ductility compared to hcp.. Limitations: The study did not investigate possible phonon instabilities during the relaxation of the computational cell.. Future work: The authors propose that the findings provide atomic-level knowledge for the intelligent design of further high-entropy materials.. Quote: "The hcp phase possesses more than two times larger intrinsic strength than that of the fcc phase."

card: Paper card. Question: How do semi-coherent phase boundaries and the proportion of FCC/BCC phases influence the strengthening mechanism and mechanical properties in a eutectic dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and AlCoCrFeNi2.4 (eutectic dual-phase HEA with BCC and FCC lamellar phases). Processing: Vacuum arc melting of pure elements (Al, Co, Ni, Cr, Fe) at 1773 K, repeated melting at least five times with electromagnetic stirring, and solidification in a water-cooled copper hearth; some samples were cold rolled for pre-straining.. Test conditions: In situ tensile tests inside a TEM at a strain rate of ~1.0 μm∙s−1 with 200 kV accelerating voltage; room-temperature tensile tests using an Instron 5569 machine at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1.. Findings: Decreasing the proportion of the hard BCC phase increased the overall strength due to potent impediments from chemically disordered semi-coherent phase boundaries.; The as-casted sample exhibited a fracture strength of ~0.94 GPa and ductility of ~25%.; Pre-straining the alloy increased the yield strength by a factor of ~5.; Increasing the volume fraction of BCC phase from 0.3 (Ni2.4) to 0.45 (Ni2.1) decreased the ultimate strength from 0.86 GPa to 0.97 GPa.; Dense dislocation walls formed along phase boundaries within the FCC phase, acting as strong barriers to dislocation motion.; The orientation relationship between phases was identified as (1–11)FCC//(01–1)BCC and [011]FCC//[111]BCC (K-S relationship).; A narrow segregation zone of randomly distributed Cr atoms, typically less than 2 nm in width, was detected near the phase boundary.. Mechanism: The authors argue that semi-coherent phase boundaries decorated with chemically disordered multiple elements act as potent obstacles, causing dense dislocation storage in the FCC phase. This, combined with massive cross-slip and the formation of dislocation substructures (walls and networks) in the FCC phase, leads to exceptional work hardening and strength, making the FCC phase the primary contributor to strengthening rather than just the hard BCC phase.. Limitations: The authors note that a critical limit presumably exists in the proportion of two phases, beyond which the overall strength would decrease with more FCC phases due to the failure of second phase strengthening.. Future work: The authors propose that their findings shed light on new ways to optimize mechanical properties by tuning the proportion of pre-strained FCC phases and leveraging the unique deformation mechanisms of dual-phase HEAs.. Quote: "decreasing the proportion of BCC phase in fact increased the strength due to the existence of chemically disordered semi-coherent phase boundaries"

card: Paper card. Question: How does the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallics within the fcc phase of a eutectic Al0.7CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy influence its strain-rate dependent mechanical behavior, specifically yield strength, work hardening, and deformation mechanisms under quasi-static versus dynamic loading?. System: Al0.7CoCrFeNi (15 at.% Al, 21.25 at.% each of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni) forming a lamellar dual-phase microstructure of fcc + B2 (with B2 containing bcc nano-precipitates), further modified by L12 precipitation in the fcc phase.. Processing: Melting of elemental constituents, homogenization at 1150 °C for 1 h, cold rolling to 30% reduction, annealing at 1100 °C for 5 mins (CR-H condition), and low-temperature annealing at 580 °C for 24 h (CR-H-580 condition).. Test conditions: Quasi-static tensile loading at a strain rate of 10−3 s−1 and dynamic compressive loading using a split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) at a strain rate of 2 × 103 s−1.. Findings: The CR-H-580 condition with L12 precipitates exhibited a yield strength of ~1080 MPa and UTS of ~1370 MPa under quasi-static loading, compared to ~770 MPa YS and ~1090 MPa UTS for the CR-H condition.; Under dynamic loading (2 × 103 s−1), flow stresses reached ~1800 MPa for the CR-H-580 condition without failure up to 20% strain.; The introduction of L12 precipitates resulted in a precipitation strengthening of ~310 MPa, which compares reasonably well with the Orowan model prediction of ~360 MPa.; The steady-state work hardening rate increased from ~3000 MPa in the CR-H condition to >4000 MPa in the CR-H-580 condition.; The strain rate sensitivity (SRS) parameter (m) at 1% flow stress was 0.018 for CR-H and 0.017 for CR-H-580, indicating L12 precipitation did not significantly alter SRS.; Post-deformation analysis revealed that the L12 phase disorders under both quasi-static and dynamic deformation, forming anti-phase boundaries.; High density of twins (approx. 20 nm thick) was observed in the fcc phase under dynamic testing, whereas only fine-scale nano-twins were seen under quasi-static testing.; APT analysis showed L12 precipitates have a radius of ~3–5 nm, a volume fraction of ~9.5% within the fcc lamellae, and a composition of ~56.4 at.% Ni and ~35.8 at.% Al.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the strength increase to the Orowan dislocation bowing and bypass mechanism by coherent L12 precipitates. The high work hardening is explained by the capability of the lamellar structure to store high dislocation densities at interfaces and the formation of anti-phase boundaries upon L12 disordering. The lack of significant change in SRS is rationalized by the presence of precipitate-free channels near the lamellar boundaries which act as sites for high dislocation storage, and the thermally activated nature of the coherent L12 precipitates.. Limitations: The text notes that detailed first-principles computational studies are needed to establish the exact site-occupancies of elements within the ordered L12 structure due to the unusually high Al content. It also mentions that the B2 lamellae are not continuous but pinched off at the microscopic scale.. Future work: The authors state that detailed first-principles, electronic structure based computational studies need to be coupled with experimental observations to establish the site-occupancies of different elements within the ordered L12 structure.. Quote: "Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the mechanical behavior and resistance to shear localization of the single-phase fcc Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy under high strain-rate dynamic loading?. System: Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (single phase fcc). Processing: Vacuum-induction melting to cast a plate (~127 mm × 305 mm × 19 mm), followed by hot-isostatic-pressing (HIP) at 1,204 °C and 103 MPa for 4 hours, homogenization at 1,200 °C for 2 hours, and water quench.. Test conditions: Quasi-static compression (strain rate 10−4 s−1), dynamic compression using Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar (strain rates up to 1800 s−1 and 104 s−1), and forced shear localization using hat-shaped specimens at high strain rates.. Findings: Yield stress increases from 216 MPa to 503 MPa as strain rate increases from 10−4 s−1 to 1.8 × 102 s−1.; Strain-rate sensitivity (m) is approximately 0.053, which is double that of coarse-grained pure aluminum (0.028).; The strain hardening rate of the alloy exceeds 1000 MPa, significantly higher than that of coarse-grained pure aluminum.; No adiabatic shear band was observed in hat-shaped samples subjected to an imposed shear strain of ~1.1.; At a strain rate of 104 s−1 and true strain of 0.5, the calculated temperature rise is only 109 K (to 402 K).; Mechanical twins with a ~36% area fraction and ~2.4 μm average thickness were observed in the deformed region.; Dynamic recrystallization was absent in the forced shear region, indicating the material continued to harden rather than soften.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the combination of solid solution hardening, forest dislocation hardening, and mechanical twinning creates an excellent work hardening ability that suppresses shear localization. This high strain hardening ability, coupled with high strain-rate sensitivity and modest thermal softening, prevents the thermal softening from overcoming strain hardening, thereby inhibiting the formation of adiabatic shear bands.. Limitations: The authors state that adiabatic shear localization of this alloy can only be activated by higher strains and temperatures than those imposed by their experiments.. Quote: "The combination of multiple strengthening mechanisms such as solid solution hardening, forest dislocation hardening, as well as mechanical twinning leads to a high work hardening rate"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the limited ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) be overcome to achieve ultra-ductility while maintaining high strength?. System: Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2 (at%) eutectic high-entropy alloy consisting of FCC and B2 phases; industrial A357 casting aluminum alloy. Processing: Two cycles of 30% cold rolling followed by annealing at 1200 °C for 20 mins with water quenching; for A357: two cycles of 15% cold rolling at 540 °C for 40 mins followed by two cycles of 30% cold rolling at 540 °C for 40 mins. Test conditions: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature with an initial strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; in situ tensile tests in FE-SEM; loading-unloading-reloading tests for back stress measurement. Findings: The phase-selectively recrystallized (PSR) EHEA achieves a uniform elongation of ∼33% and an engineering ultimate tensile strength approaching ∼2.2 GPa.; The PSR EHEA exhibits a fracture true strain of ∼30%, which is double that of the As-cast (AC) alloy (∼14%) and the fully recrystallized (FR) alloy (∼17%).; The fracture true stress of the PSR EHEA reaches ∼1850 MPa, significantly higher than the AC (∼1390 MPa) and FR (∼1460 MPa) alloys.; The microcrack density in the fractured PSR specimen is only one-third of that in the FR specimen, even under a twofold nominal strain.; The local von Mises strain in the FCC phase can be up to 6 times higher than that in the B2 phase during deformation.; A back stress of ∼900 MPa near failure was quantitatively measured in the PSR EHEA, accounting for its high strain hardening capacity.; A B2 → body-centered tetragonal (BCT) phase transformation was observed in the PSR EHEA during deformation, with the crystal structure expanding ∼6% along the (200) direction.; The PSR strategy increased the elongation of the A357 aluminum alloy from ∼8% to ∼23% and doubled its tensile strength to ∼400 MPa.. Mechanism: Phase-selective recrystallization (PSR) eliminates weak boundaries (lamellar phase boundaries in AC and high-density grain boundaries in FR) by inducing complete recrystallization in the soft FCC phase while maintaining a skeletal, non-recrystallized B2 phase that undergoes only recovery. This microstructure prevents premature crack nucleation at weak interfaces, allowing both phases to contribute to strain hardening simultaneously through high-density dislocation multiplication and a strain-induced B2 to BCT phase transformation, thereby exhausting the alloy's strain hardening capacity before fracture.. Limitations: The proposed model for calculating the suitable deformation level for PSR is semi-quantitative because it ignores information on microstructure and strain rate.. Future work: Further modifications to the theoretical model to include microstructure and strain rate information; direct characterization of PSR behaviors under different rolling amounts and subsequent annealing to overcome the complexity of acquiring parameter values.. Quote: "The PSR EHEA with a well-tailored PSR microstructure doubles the fracture strain to ∼30%."

card: Paper card. Question: How can fatigue life be enhanced in high-entropy alloys at low strain amplitudes without sacrificing ductility, specifically by addressing the trade-off between fatigue strength and fatigue-crack-initiation resistance in precipitation-strengthened alloys?. System: Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy containing an FCC matrix and multicomponent B2 precipitates (NiAl-type). Processing: Vacuum-induction melting to fabricate a large plate, followed by hot rolling with 60% reduction at 1150 °C, and annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h. Test conditions: Monotonic tension at RT with a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; fully-reversed strain-controlled low-cycle fatigue (LCF) at RT with strain amplitudes from ±0.1% to ±1.75% and a strain rate of 1 × 10−2 s−1; real-time in situ neutron diffraction at strain amplitudes of ±0.5%, ±1%, and ±1.75%. Findings: The alloy exhibits at least four times longer fatigue life than conventional alloys at a plastic strain amplitude of ~0.03%.; The B2 phase bears significantly more stress than the FCC phase after yielding, with lattice strains nearly ten times larger.; Stress-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT) occurs in the B2 phase, evidenced by abnormal peak broadening and peak separation in neutron diffraction.; Deformation twinning is observed in the FCC matrix only at high strain amplitudes (≥1.75%), not at intermediate amplitudes (1%).; The B2 phase is plastically deformable at all tested strain amplitudes, storing dislocations and relieving stress concentration.; Fine B2 precipitates act as efficient crack arresters, forming blunted cracks, whereas coarse band-like B2 precipitates initiate microcracks.; The multicomponent B2 phase has lower antiphase boundary (APB) energies (e.g., compared to 0.697 eV/m² for pure NiAl) enabling plastic deformation.. Mechanism: The enhanced fatigue life is attributed to the ductile-transformable character of the multicomponent B2 precipitates, which undergo reversible martensitic transformation and plastic deformation to accommodate strain incompatibility with the FCC matrix. This mechanism relieves stress concentration at phase boundaries, retards microcrack initiation, and provides alternative deformation pathways, unlike brittle traditional intermetallics.. Limitations: The study notes that if the B2 phase size is too large (e.g., band-like precipitates), it becomes easy to initiate microcracks due to longer incoherent interfaces where stress concentration cannot be effectively accommodated.. Future work: The authors propose that the design strategy of introducing ductile-transformable multicomponent intermetallic precipitates can guide the design of fatigue-resistant alloys by tuning HEA compositions and thermomechanical processing.. Quote: "the current HEA shows at least four times longer life than conventional alloys"

Question: How do the surface morphology, particle size distribution, and microstructure of AlCoCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy powders evolve during mechanical alloying, and what are the resulting coating properties when deposited via atmospheric plasma spraying?. System: AlCoCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy (equimolar mixture of Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Si elemental powders). Processing: Mechanical alloying in a high-energy planetary ball mill (QM-3SP2) at 300 r·min−1, ball-to-powder weight ratio 10:1, powder loading 90 g for 5, 10, 20, and 30 h; coating deposition via atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) using 10 h milled powder, 45 kW arc power, 100 mm spray distance, 200 mm·s−1 traverse speed, with argon primary gas (0.4 MPa) and nitrogen secondary gas (0.3 MPa). Test conditions: Room temperature microhardness testing (200 g load, 10 s dwell); wear testing using a Si3N4 ball (Φ 5 mm) at 5 N load, 573 r·min−1 rotation speed, 5 mm friction radius, for 30 min; XRD (2θ 20–90°, 3°·min−1); FESEM and TEM characterization. Findings: Particle size first increased then decreased with milling time; at 10 h, a narrow peak range from several micrometers to about 50 μm was obtained.; At 10 h milling, simple body-centered cubic (BCC) and face-centered cubic (FCC) solid solution phases were formed with an average grain size of 11.7 nm and lattice strain of about 0.73%.; After plasma spraying, the lamellar structure inside a single particle disappeared, and an ordered BCC phase was detected while Si diffraction peaks vanished.; Transmission electron microscopy revealed nanometer crystalline grains with a grain size of about 30 nm in the APS coating.; The coating exhibited an average microhardness of 612 ± 41 HV.; The volume wear rate of the coating was (0.38 ± 0.08) × 10−4 mm3·N−1·m−1, approximately half that of a previously studied AlCoCrFeNiTi coating.; Wear mechanisms included adhesive wear, tribo-oxidation wear, and slight abrasion wear.; The coefficient of friction reached a steady state average of 0.57 ± 0.02 after an initial running-in stage of 6 min.. Mechanism: During mechanical alloying, plastic deformation and cold welding dominate initially, increasing particle size, followed by work hardening and fracture which reduce particle size and refine the lamellar structure. During plasma spraying, high temperatures cause melting and elemental rearrangement, leading to the disappearance of the lamellar structure, formation of an ordered BCC phase, and dissolution of Si elemental peaks. The high hardness and formation of hard tribofilms contribute to the coating's good wear resistance.. Limitations: The text notes that unmelted and semi-melted particles were present in the coating due to stochastic heating, and that limited interlamellar bonding ratio (less than one third) in thermally sprayed coatings can deteriorate mechanical properties.. Future work: The authors state the coating is promising for use in abrasive environments in industries such as petroleum, power, and mining, implying future application in these sectors.. Quote: "At the milling time of 10 h, simple body-centered cubic (BCC) and face-centered cubic (FCC) solid solution phases were formed."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the processing temperature (77 K vs. 300 K) during high-pressure torsion (HPT) affect the microstructure evolution, phase stability, and mechanical properties (hardness and tensile strength) of the Co20Cr26Fe20Mn20Ni14 high-entropy alloy, particularly regarding the phenomenon of natural aging?. System: Co20Cr26Fe20Mn20Ni14 high-entropy alloy (low stacking fault energy of 3.5 mJ/m2). Processing: High-pressure torsion (HPT) at 77 K (cryogenic) and 300 K (room temperature) under 5 GPa pressure for 1, 3, and 5 anvil turns; samples held for natural aging up to two months.. Test conditions: Vickers hardness (300 g load, 10 s dwell) measured at 10 min, 1 day, 2 weeks, 1 month, and 2 months post-processing; tensile testing (strain rate 10^-3 s^-1) conducted 2 weeks post-processing; XRD, SEM, EBSD, and TEM analysis performed.. Findings: Cryogenic HPT resulted in lower mechanical strength (hardness and tensile strength) compared to room temperature HPT after natural aging.; Vickers hardness of cryo-HPT samples dropped precipitously after two weeks of natural aging, whereas room temperature HPT samples showed no hardness decrease over one month.; Deformation-induced FCC-to-HCP phase transformation occurred in the alloy processed by cryo-HPT, confirmed by XRD and TEM.; Dislocation density in cryo-HPT samples was very high (~1.0 to 2.5 × 10^16 m^-2) immediately after processing but decreased significantly with natural aging time.; Room temperature HPT produced an average grain size of 61 ± 25 nm, while cryo-HPT resulted in larger average grain sizes (e.g., 5.42 ± 1.69 μm after 5 turns).; The volume fraction of deformation twins decreased from 48% in the annealed state to 0.6% after 5 turns of cryo-HPT.; The σ phase peaks observed in the annealed state almost disappeared after HPT processing at both 77 K and 300 K.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the lower strength and hardness drop in cryo-HPT samples to 'self-annealing' (static recovery and static recrystallization) during natural aging, driven by the high stored energy from deformation and the low stacking fault energy which inhibits cross-slip and dynamic recrystallization during processing but allows static recovery afterward. The FCC-to-HCP transformation is rationalized as a kinetically possible transition due to high pressure and low temperature overcoming the energy barrier.. Limitations: The authors note that extreme grain refinement during cryo-HPT cannot be entirely ruled out, as nano-grained structures might have been unstable at room temperature and underwent recovery before characterization.. Quote: "Cryogenic HPT was found to result in a lower mechanical strength of alloy Co20Cr26Fe20Mn20Ni14 than room temperature HPT."

card: Paper card. Question: How can yield strength be enhanced in metastable austenitic steels without sacrificing ductility, specifically by utilizing dislocation strengthening mechanisms that do not impede the nucleation of new dislocations required for plastic deformation?. System: Commercial AISI 301 (EN1.4310) metastable austenitic steel. Processing: One-step thermal mechanical treatment (TMT) via hot rolling at 450 °C with thickness reductions of 10% and 20%; initial material was solid solution treated at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at a strain rate of 1×10−3 s−1; in-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) at 200 kV using a stepwise displacement loading mode.. Findings: Yield strength increased from 322 ± 18 MPa to 675 ± 15 MPa with 20% thickness reduction.; Uniform elongation increased from 54% ± 3% to 71% ± 2% with 20% thickness reduction.; Dislocation density reached approximately 10^15 m−2 in the sample with 20% reduction.; No grain boundaries or cellular substructures were introduced by the optimized TMT process.; Phase transformation (α-martensite) nucleated at an earlier stage of deformation in TMT samples compared to solid solution treated samples.; Martensite growth terminated at high-angle grain boundaries or twin boundaries due to coherency dependence.; Lamella spacing between intercalated α-martensite and austenite was approximately 500 nm before fracture.. Mechanism: The success relies on decoupled strengthening and toughening mechanisms where yield strength is controlled by the initial dislocation density (which impedes motion), while ductility is retained because the pre-stored dislocations do not pin phase boundaries but instead promote phase transformation and serve as effective dislocation sources via stress singularities at terraced phase boundaries, allowing new dislocations to be nucleated to carry plastic deformation.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that the complexity of the underlying mechanism may require further investigation.. Future work: The authors suggest that following the guideline of decoupling strengthening and toughening mechanisms, other methods may be developed to enhance material performance in metal manufacturing.. Quote: "yield strength is controlled by initial dislocation density while ductility is retained by the capability to nucleate new dislocations to carry plastic deformation."

card: Paper card. Question: Is polymorphism still possible in entropy-stabilized high-entropy alloys (HEAs) that are generally believed to possess extremely high structural stability and maintain a single-phase structure?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (Cantor's alloy). Processing: Synthesized via gas-atomization (melt injected into high purity Ar at 4 MPa pressure); subjected to hydrostatic compression up to ~41 GPa using a diamond anvil cell (DAC) with helium as pressure-transmitting medium; subsequently heated using resistive heating (up to 723 K) or double-sided Nd:YLF laser heating (up to ~1,400 K) at various pressures (6, 14, 26 GPa).. Test conditions: Room temperature compression up to ~41 GPa; heating at ambient pressure up to 723 K; heating at 6, 14, and 26 GPa up to ~1,400 K; in situ synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring.. Findings: The fcc-to-hcp polymorphic transition starts at approximately 22 GPa and almost completes at approximately 41 GPa.; The phase transition is irreversible; the hcp phase is retained when pressure is released to ambient conditions.; The hcp phase remains stable up to 633 K at ambient pressure before transforming back to fcc.; At 26 GPa, the critical temperature for the hcp-to-fcc transition is approximately 1,400 K.; The isothermal bulk modulus (B0) is 153.9±3.0 GPa for the fcc phase and 150.2±4.6 GPa for the hcp phase.; The c/a ratio of the hcp phase remained almost constant at 1.62±0.01 during compression and decompression.; The transition is sluggish, with fcc and hcp phases coexisting over a wide pressure range of ~22 to ~41 GPa.; Decompression from different maximum pressures yields fcc/hcp composites with tunable fractions.. Mechanism: The transition occurs because the hcp structure is thermodynamically more favorable at lower temperatures and high pressures, while the fcc phase is stable at higher temperatures and lower pressures; the transition is kinetically hindered by high energy barriers and low stacking fault energy (~20 mJ m−2), requiring high pressure to overcome these barriers to form the hcp phase.. Limitations: The transition is sluggish and irreversible, making it difficult to determine the real equilibrium phase boundary (Clapeyron coexistence curve) experimentally; grain size was not small enough for statistically reliable Rietveld refinement of volume fractions; overshooting often exists due to high energy barriers.. Future work: The authors suggest that this behavior could be general in various HEAs and propose new avenues for tailoring HEA properties via polymorphic transition-induced HEA composites, particularly at cryogenic temperatures where transition pressure could be largely decreased.. Quote: "The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures."
